prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Keywords: Ring, The, For

outputs.L1:
Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky,  
The flying cloud, the frosty light:  
The year is dying in the night;  
Ring out, wild bells, and let him die.

Ring out the old, ring in the new,  
Ring, happy bells, across the snow:  
The year is going, let him go;  
Ring out the false, ring in the true.

Ring out the grief that saps the mind  
For those that here we see no more;  
Ring out the feud of rich and poor,  
Ring in redress to all mankind.

Ring out a slowly dying cause,  
And ancient forms of party strife;  
Ring in the nobler modes of life,  
With sweeter manners, purer laws.

Ring out the want, the care, the sin,  
The faithless coldness of the times;  
Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes,  
But ring the fuller minstrel in.

Ring out false pride in place and blood,  
The civic slander and the spite;  
Ring in the love of truth and right,  
Ring in the common love of good.

Ring out old shapes of foul disease;  
Ring out the narrowing lust of gold;  
Ring out the thousand wars of old,  
Ring in the thousand years of peace.

Ring in the valiant man and free,  
The larger heart, the kindlier hand;  
Ring out the darkness of the land,  
Ring in the Christ that is to be.
outputs.L2:
Sound loudly, untamed bells, beneath the stormy heavens,  
beneath the racing clouds and the icy brightness.  
The old year is passing away in the night;  
clang, wild bells, and allow it to depart.

Let the past be driven out, and welcome what is new.  
Peal, joyful bells, over the snow-covered land.  
The year is leaving; do not hold it back.  
Send away what is false, and bring in what is true.

Drive out the sorrow that weakens the heart and mind  
for those we once saw here but see no longer.  
End the hostility between wealth and poverty,  
and bring justice and repair to all humanity.

Let a fading cause be dismissed,  
along with outdated kinds of political conflict.  
Welcome higher and better ways of living,  
with gentler conduct and cleaner, fairer laws.

Banish need, anxiety, wrongdoing,  
and the cold disloyal spirit of the age.  
Let my sad verses be sounded out and ended,  
but let a richer, stronger song begin.

Cast out hollow pride in rank and ancestry,  
along with public slander and bitterness.  
Bring in devotion to truth and justice,  
and a shared love of what is good.

Send away the old forms of terrible sickness.  
Drive out the cramped greed for gold.  
End the countless wars of the past,  
and usher in a long age of peace.

Welcome the brave and free human being,  
the broader heart and the gentler hand.  
Dispel the darkness covering the land,  
and bring in the Christ who is yet to come.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents a powerful call for transition, urging the old year to pass away and the new year to arrive with hope, renewal, and moral purpose. It treats the turning of the year not merely as a change in time, but as an opportunity for society to leave behind what is harmful and begin again with clearer values and higher ideals.

At its heart, the poem asks humanity to cast out falsehood, grief, inequality, and conflict. The passing year becomes a symbol of everything that has burdened people: dishonesty, sorrow, social injustice, and division. By calling for these things to be removed, the poem expresses a deep desire for healing and a more truthful, compassionate world.

The poem also urges society to abandon outdated causes, political strife, and corrupt social habits. It suggests that old ways of thinking and living have caused suffering and must give way to nobler forms of conduct. Instead of clinging to selfish ambitions or destructive disputes, people are encouraged to embrace a more generous, ethical, and humane way of life.

Throughout the poem, there is a strong rejection of pride, slander, greed, disease, and war. These forces are presented as obstacles to human progress and spiritual well-being. In their place, the poem calls for truth, justice, kindness, and peace. It imagines a society where people act with honesty, care for one another, and seek harmony rather than conflict.

Ultimately, the poem envisions a better future marked by freedom, compassion, moral light, and spiritual renewal. The new year represents the possibility of transformation, both for individuals and for society as a whole. Through its repeated calls to let go of the old and welcome the new, the poem becomes a hopeful prayer for a world guided by goodness, wisdom, and peace.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the turning of the year as more than a simple change in the calendar. It treats the New Year as a powerful moment of renewal, when humanity is invited to leave behind the suffering and failures of the past and move toward a better moral and social future. Through the repeated image of bells ringing across the winter night, the poem creates a sense of ceremony, as if the whole world is being called to take part in a symbolic act of cleansing and transformation.

The bells are central to the poem’s meaning. They “ring out” the old year, but they also ring out everything associated with sorrow, corruption, and human weakness. The speaker wants the bells to drive away grief, falsehood, pride, selfishness, injustice, class conflict, war, and despair. In this way, the sound of the bells becomes almost purifying. They are not merely marking midnight; they are imagined as a force that can shake society awake and help it cast off the darkness of the past.

At the same time, the poem asks the bells to “ring in” a better world. The speaker calls for truth, peace, kindness, justice, courage, and moral responsibility to replace the evils that have dominated the old year. The New Year becomes a symbol of hope, not just for individual happiness but for collective reform. The poem imagines a society in which people are guided by compassion rather than greed, unity rather than division, and spiritual faith rather than bitterness or doubt.

The contrast between the old and the new gives the poem much of its emotional power. The old year is connected with pain, conflict, and moral failure, while the new year represents possibility and renewal. Yet the poem is not simply optimistic in a shallow way. It recognizes that the world is troubled and that human beings have caused much suffering. Its hope is serious and urgent: the speaker longs for real change in human behavior, social relationships, and spiritual values.

Ultimately, the poem turns the arrival of the New Year into a vision of collective transformation. It suggests that humanity can move from darkness into light if it rejects cruelty, dishonesty, and division and embraces truth, justice, peace, and love. The ringing bells therefore become a symbol of both farewell and welcome: farewell to the grief and corruption of the past, and welcome to a future shaped by moral renewal and spiritual hope.
outputs.L5:
**The Ring for a Promise**

The ring is more than a simple piece of jewelry. For many people, it represents love, commitment, and memories that last a lifetime. Whether it is given for an engagement, a wedding, or a special celebration, the ring often carries a meaning far greater than its size or value.

For some, the ring is a symbol of unity. Its circular shape has no beginning and no end, reminding us of loyalty, connection, and lasting devotion. The person who wears it may see it every day and remember the promise, the moment, or the person behind it.

The ring can also be a gift for hope. It may mark a new chapter, a personal achievement, or a bond between two people. No matter the occasion, the ring remains a powerful symbol, showing that even the smallest object can hold the deepest meaning.
